analysis.one_liner: Freezes cable TV rates until the FCC studies why they kept rising.
analysis.headline: The bill to freeze cable rates died in a House committee without ever getting a vote, despite 16 sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Cable TV bills had risen steadily after the 1996 law that loosened federal rate controls. This bill ordered the FCC, within ten days, to bar cable companies from raising basic cable or cable programming rates above their October 1, 1997 levels. The freeze would stay in place until Congress acted after the FCC reported on what drove the 1992-1997 increases and whether competition could be extended to restrain them. The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its telecommunications subcommittee, where no action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that subscribe to cable television would have gotten a break on their monthly bills, since the freeze covered both basic service and pay channels bundled as cable programming services [S2] [S3]. Consumers generally would have gained an official accounting of why cable prices rose so fast in the five years after the 1992 rate rules were loosened, plus a roadmap for extending competition [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Within ten days of enactment, the FCC would have had to order cable operators to stop imposing or collecting any increase above their October 1, 1997 rates for basic cable service and cable programming services [S2] [S3].
The freeze would have remained in effect until Congress passed a law acting on the FCC's report, so rates could not simply resume climbing when the study ended [S2] [S3].

The FCC would have had to investigate the causes of rate increases from October 1992 to October 1997, whether competition had actually restrained them, and what steps could extend competition and eliminate unjust or unreasonable rates [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators would have been barred from raising rates above October 1997 levels, giving up revenue growth they had been collecting from subscribers [S2] [S3]. Investors in cable companies would have borne the cost of the earnings hit. The FCC would have absorbed the cost of running the inquiry and writing the report.

drawbacks.text: A rate freeze does not create competition. It holds prices down by order while the FCC studies the market, so consumers get relief but no guarantee that lower prices last once Congress legislates again [S2] [S3].

The freeze was open-ended until a future act of Congress, which could block cable operators from recovering genuine cost increases or from funding new service investments during that period [S2] [S3].
Freezing rates for both basic and cable programming services could discourage investment in new channels and services, a trade-off an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers, the bill offered direct, immediate relief on a monthly bill almost everyone paid, at a modest cost spread across cable operators and investors, with the uncertainty falling on operators rather than the public. The main weakness is that a freeze treats the symptom while the FCC study looks for the cure, and an indefinite freeze set by one Congress could hamper operators' ability to fund service improvements. On balance, the bill's costs were concentrated and its benefits broad, which is why the cable industry would have fought it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Commerce Committee's telecommunications subcommittee from November 1997 until the Congress ended in January 1999, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio of Oregon, joined by Rep. Maurice Hinchey, introduced the Cable Rate Moratorium Act on October 29, 1997 [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce, then on November 9, 1997 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S1] [S5].
Fifteen members cosponsored the bill, 14 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never left the subcommittee and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators are better off because the bill never passed: they kept free rein to raise rates above their October 1997 levels, and no FCC inquiry was ever mandated. Cable subscribers never got the freeze or the study.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cable Rate Moratorium Act directing the FCC to freeze cable rates and study the causes of past increases.

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Joined DeFazio in introducing the bill on October 29, 1997.

for.name: 15 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; no markup, hearing, or vote on it was ever scheduled, and the bill sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Cable television industry
against.role: Cable operators affected by the rate freeze
against.what_they_did: Would have lost the ability to raise rates above October 1997 levels if the bill passed; no member of Congress is recorded as speaking against the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the record shows only that the bill's sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; opposition appears in the record only as the absence of committee action under a Republican chair.

industries.note: The bill would have barred cable operators from collecting any rate increase above October 1997 levels, cutting off the revenue growth they had been earning from subscribers. Operators' gain from the bill's failure is subscribers' continued rising bills.

industries.industry: FCC-regulated cable programming services (pay channel bundlers and network programmers)
industries.note: Programmers who sell channels through cable packages would have faced a frozen price environment that limited revenue growth and could slow investment in new channels, though the bill also ordered a study of whether competition could be extended, which could open new distribution paths.
